PullRequest.Title: VS code remote tunnel terminal in external terminal

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The signal handler, awaited setup requests, default 30-second timeout, and lack of cancellation propagation are all explicit in the changed code. Only how often a remote host stalls is uncertain.
Findings.PerformanceResource: A pending WebSocket JSON-RPC request and, during createTerminal, a potentially running remote shell process
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cancellation latency grows to the remaining timeout of whichever initialize, createTerminal, or subscribe request is active, up to the shared 30-second default.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Blocked CLI termination and delayed remote-shell cleanup
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no standalone runTerminal setup path or signal handler that could enter these timeout-bound RPC waits.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP handlers only resolve the separate completion promise via finish(), while setup remains synchronously awaited in initialize, createTerminal, or subscribe.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added termination handler at line 181 records completion but does not abort the newly added timeout-bound setup requests at lines 195, 207, and 217.
Findings.Title: Abort in-flight setup RPCs on termination
Findings.Impact: If the agent host is slow or stops replying during setup, Ctrl+C or process termination appears ignored for as long as 30 seconds. If createTerminal was already sent, cleanup is also deferred while the remote shell may continue running.
Findings.Evidence: Line 181 calls finish() only. The same function is still awaiting client.request at lines 195, 207, or 217; ProtocolClient.request has no AbortSignal and uses the 30,000 ms default timeout, so finish() cannot settle the active await. The outer setup abort handlers are removed before runTerminal is invoked.
Findings.Recommendation: Give the terminal session an AbortController and make ProtocolClient.request/deadline accept it, aborting the pending setup await on these signals; retain the disposeTerminal request when creation may already have reached the server.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The event-to-WebSocket-to-PTY/headless-terminal call path and the repository's established debounce for reflow are explicit. Exact event rate varies by terminal host and drag behavior, affecting magnitude rather than mechanism.
Findings.PerformanceResource: WebSocket messages, server state reductions, native PTY resize calls, and headless-terminal reflow CPU
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cost grows with every grid-size event while a window is dragged, and each horizontal resize becomes more expensive as the remote terminal's scrollback grows.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Excess network/CPU work and resize jank for long-running terminals
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR the standalone client emitted no resize traffic. The existing VS Code terminal path routes layout changes through TerminalResizeDebouncer, using a 100 ms debounce for costly horizontal reflow once scrollback is nontrivial.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every stdout resize event immediately dispatches a terminal/resized protocol action, including repeated intermediate dimensions, with no deduplication or coalescing.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added onResize callback at line 169 sends one protocol action synchronously for each local resize event rather than retaining and flushing the latest dimensions.
Findings.Title: Coalesce terminal resize actions
Findings.Impact: Dragging a terminal window after accumulating scrollback can generate a burst of round trips and remote reflows, making resize and terminal interaction stutter.
Findings.Evidence: Line 169 dispatches directly from the resize event. AgentHostTerminalManager handles each TerminalResized envelope by calling both terminal.pty.resize() and terminal.headlessTerminal.resize(); the platform's TerminalResizeDebouncer documents horizontal resize as expensive due to reflow and debounces it by 100 ms.
Findings.Recommendation: Send the initial dimensions immediately, then deduplicate identical dimensions and debounce/coalesce subsequent resize events to the latest cols/rows (with a final flush on quiescence/teardown).

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: Both timeout values and their strict sequential ordering are explicit, and the server contract confirms disposal releases the remote process. The uncertain factor is how often users exit with a slow-output backlog.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Queued terminal output, an unnecessarily live remote shell process, and a subsequent network cleanup RPC
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Shutdown delay grows with queued output and local terminal drain speed up to 5 seconds, then adds the disposeTerminal RPC's separate timeout of up to another 5 seconds.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Increased exit latency and delayed release of the remote process
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no standalone session cleanup sequence that serialized local terminal draining ahead of remote process disposal.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new finally block first waits up to five seconds for local output and the keyboard-mode reset to flush, restores input mode, and only then sends disposeTerminal at line 290.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added await at line 273 places the bounded local-output flush directly before, and therefore serializes it with, the added remote cleanup request at line 290.
Findings.Title: Start remote disposal before waiting for local output
Findings.Impact: When a user presses Ctrl+] or terminates during heavy output on a slow terminal, the command can remain open for up to roughly 10 seconds and the remote shell keeps running throughout the first wait, even though remote disposal is independent of the required local write ordering.
Findings.Evidence: Line 273 awaits a 5,000 ms local drain. The disposeTerminal request is not started until line 290 and has its own 5,000 ms timeout. The protocol contract states disposeTerminal kills the process if it is still running, while the local reset only needs to precede restoring cooked input.
Findings.Recommendation: Start the disposeTerminal request as soon as cleanup begins and await it alongside the local flush; keep the keyboard reset flush ordered before setRawMode(wasRaw), but do not make remote process cleanup wait on local rendering.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: A fresh Node process loads the static application/SDK module graph, parses arguments, and writes help or validation output. No authentication, subprocess, or network call occurs after --help is recognized, but static module loading is on the critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Node resolves and reads the application plus Dev Tunnels/WebSocket dependency module graph before main() checks --help.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One fixed module graph per CLI process; no input-dependent fan-out.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The standalone command and its module graph did not exist before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before help or validation output can be printed.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Fixed application and dependency module graph per invocation; argument count is small and bounded.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Node ESM loading and argument handling are effectively serial.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no application cache across CLI processes; warm OS filesystem cache may reduce module-read cost.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High that static imports execute before help; low evidence that their fixed cost is materially user-visible.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Dependency module-load duration on supported machines was not measured.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: eager loading is observable but the diff provides no evidence of a material startup regression rather than ordinary bounded CLI initialization.

Scenarios.CriticalPath: Credential acquisition completes first, followed by one logical Dev Tunnels list operation; selection or --list output cannot proceed before both finish.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run gh auth token for the default GitHub credential path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one subprocess per launch on this path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone authentication subprocess existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocks discovery until the token is returned, with a 30-second timeout.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Request a device code and poll GitHub for an access token when --client-id is used.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One code request plus one paced poll per server interval until approval or expiry; only one in flight.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone device-flow network path existed before this PR.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: List authorized tunnels filtered by the launcher label through the management SDK.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One logical list call returning all matching machines; SDK pagination details are not established by repository code.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone tunnel discovery call existed before this PR.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of authorized tunnels matching the launcher label; device-flow poll count scales with user approval time and the server-provided interval.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Authentication and discovery are serial. Device-flow HTTP polls are paced and have at most one request in flight.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: TUNNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN is read directly. GitHub CLI may own a persisted login, but this client still invokes gh once per launch. Device-flow tokens and tunnel inventory are not cached by the client; failures are not negatively cached.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the subprocess/network boundaries and serial critical path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Account tunnel counts and management-service latency vary; SDK-internal pagination was not visible in the repository.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: calls are one-per-launch or server-paced, and no diff-introduced per-machine boundary fan-out was found.

Scenarios.Scenario: Connect to a selected machine and create/subscribe to a remote shell
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The selected tunnel is fetched with port/token metadata, the relay connects, port 31546 becomes available, a forwarded stream and WebSocket are opened, host selection completes when protocol 6 requires it, then initialize, createTerminal, and subscribe RPCs run serially before input becomes ready.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Get one tunnel with ports/connect token, establish the relay, wait for and connect to one forwarded port, and upgrade one WebSocket.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One selected-tunnel lookup, one relay connection, one forwarded-port stream, and one WebSocket upgrade per session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The standalone connection path did not exist before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All are serial prerequisites for host and terminal setup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Receive one host inventory, send one host selection, and await one startup acknowledgement.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One exchange for protocol-6 tunnels; no per-host network requests.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone host-selection exchange existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocks protocol initialization; dedicated startup may wait up to 120 seconds.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Location: Remote agent-host startup reached by experimental/tunnel-terminal-client/src/tunnel.ts selectHost
ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: When explicitly chosen, request creation of one dedicated remote agent host, which may download/start server components.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one explicitly selected dedicated host per session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The client did not previously request dedicated-host creation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remote startup acknowledgement blocks shell setup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send initialize, createTerminal, and subscribe JSON-RPC requests over the WebSocket.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly three serial setup RPCs for a successful session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The standalone terminal setup RPC sequence did not exist before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Input is not enabled until all three complete.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One selected machine and one selected host. Host inventory size affects only local parsing/picker output. Dedicated-host startup cost depends on remote provisioning and possible component download.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Management lookup, relay setup, forwarded-port connection, WebSocket upgrade, host selection, and three setup RPCs are serialized. Each RPC has one pending operation on this path.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Tunnel metadata, connect token, relay connection, host inventory, and protocol initialization are cold on every CLI launch; no cross-process cache or request coalescing exists.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for ordering, cardinality, and the uncancellable active-RPC mechanism.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Relay and dedicated-host startup times vary with network and remote state.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported: termination only settles a separate completion promise and cannot interrupt the currently awaited setup RPC, delaying cancellation by up to 30 seconds.

Scenarios.Scenario: Interactive terminal input, output, and window resizing
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Input is JSON-serialized and sent over the WebSocket to the remote PTY; output notifications are parsed and written to the local terminal. Resize events are sent to the server, reduced into terminal state, and applied to both the native PTY and headless terminal.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send terminal input actions over the tunnel WebSocket.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to one message per 4096 characters of each delivered input chunk; socket buffering is capped.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone terminal input stream existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remote shell input cannot be processed until the message crosses the relay.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Receive, copy/decode, and parse terminal JSON notifications before writing output.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One parse/dispatch per server frame; total bytes are bounded in queued and output buffers but stream lifetime is unbounded.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone terminal output stream existed before this PR.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send terminal/resized for every local resize event.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: R messages for R emitted resize events, including intermediate dimensions; no deduplication/coalescing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The standalone client emitted no resize actions; the existing workbench terminal path uses TerminalResizeDebouncer for costly reflow.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Each message triggers remote state processing and terminal resizing.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Apply each resize action to the native PTY and headless terminal.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One native PTY resize plus one headless-terminal resize per received resize action.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: This server behavior pre-existed, but the PR introduces an uncoalesced client event source that invokes it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Consumes remote CPU and can reflow accumulated scrollback while the user is dragging the window.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Input bytes, output frame count/bytes, and local resize-event count. Input is split into 4096-character actions; buffers are capped at 8 MiB. Resize cost scales with event count and remote scrollback size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The protocol read pump processes messages serially. Output writes may be in flight but tracked against an 8 MiB cap. Input and resize dispatches are synchronous and have no shared limiter or resize coalescer.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache applies. Snapshot/early output is buffered only during subscription and is bounded; live messages are streamed.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for one-action-per-event fan-out and downstream PTY/headless resize calls.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Resize event cadence and scrollback depth vary by terminal host and session lifetime.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported: uncoalesced resize actions amplify network, reducer, native PTY, and headless reflow work during window drags.

Scenarios.Scenario: Session interruption, exit, and remote cleanup
Scenarios.CriticalPath: After completion, listeners are removed, the local keyboard-mode reset and pending output are flushed, local input mode is restored, then disposeTerminal is requested and the relay is disposed by the caller.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Flush queued terminal bytes and the Win32 keyboard-mode reset to local terminal output.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One cleanup flush per session; bytes depend on outstanding output and are capped at 8 MiB.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone local terminal cleanup sequence existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Currently blocks both local return and initiation of remote shell disposal for up to 5 seconds.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send one disposeTerminal RPC that kills the remote process if still running.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one request per attempted terminal creation, with a 5-second timeout.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone remote terminal cleanup RPC existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cannot start until the preceding local flush and input restoration complete, then independently blocks return.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Close the WebSocket/forwarded stream and dispose the relay.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One relay disposal per connected session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No standalone relay lifecycle existed before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs after runTerminal cleanup and must finish before main returns.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Queued local output up to the 8 MiB cap, local terminal drain rate, and remote cleanup response latency.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The local output flush and remote dispose RPC are currently strictly serialized, each with a 5-second bound; relay disposal follows after runTerminal returns.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache applies. Cleanup state is per session and idempotence is tracked by local booleans.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for the explicit sequential waits and their timeout bounds.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: How often users exit with a slow-output backlog and how long relay disposal takes are environment-dependent.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported: remote disposal unnecessarily waits behind local rendering, producing up to roughly 10 seconds of serial shutdown latency and keeping the remote shell alive during the first wait.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 24 changed files and relevant server/workbench call paths. Submitted three findings covering setup cancellation latency, resize-event fan-out into remote reflow, and serialized local/remote cleanup. No qualifying regression-fix record was available because the old SDK mechanism is not present in the PR base.
